title: Free Plain-English Health Sites Directory
disclaimer: This directory is education only. It is never medical advice. Nothing here diagnoses, treats, or replaces a conversation with your own clinician or pharmacist.

sources.name: MedlinePlus
sources.what: The single best first stop for plain-English overviews of hundreds of health topics, drugs, supplements, and lab tests.
sources.notes: No ads, no account, no upsells. Written specifically for the general public, with Spanish versions and medical encyclopedia pages alongside.

sources.name: MedlinePlus Medical Encyclopedia
sources.what: A-Z article-and-illustration encyclopedia covering tests, symptoms, injuries, and diseases in short, readable pieces.
sources.notes: The A.D.A.M. encyclopedia licensed for public use. Short entries, clear illustrations, handy when you want a two-minute answer.

sources.name: NIH News in Health
sources.what: A free monthly newsletter translating new NIH-funded research into readable, friendly articles.
sources.notes: Great model of how to say 'what the research actually showed' without media spin. Print-friendly for clinic waiting rooms.

sources.name: National Institute on Aging (NIA)
sources.what: Deep but readable guides on Alzheimer's, caregiving, medications and aging, fitness for older adults.
sources.notes: The Alzheimer's and caregiving sections are unusually kind in tone and come in large-print-style layouts.

sources.name: NIDDK (diabetes, digestive, kidney)
sources.what: Authoritative plain-language pages on diabetes, kidney disease, digestive conditions, and weight management.
sources.notes: Their diabetes series is written for real patients; Spanish versions available for most major topics.

sources.name: NHLBI (heart, lung, blood)
sources.what: Heart-healthy eating plans (including DASH), blood pressure and cholesterol guides, sleep resources.
sources.notes: The DASH eating plan pages include printable handouts you can hand to a family member as-is.

sources.name: CDC (health topics A-Z)
sources.publisher: U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention
sources.what: Not NIH, but the other big free government health library: vaccines, infections, chronic conditions, travel health.
sources.notes: Government agency pages are federal public-domain education material; no commercial ads. Some topic pages vary in reading level.

sources.name: Cleveland Clinic Health Library
sources.what: Thousands of reviewed articles on symptoms, diseases, tests, and treatments, written by clinicians in plain English.
sources.notes: Best-in-class hospital teaching site. Some sections include clearly labeled sponsored health content, which is why ad density is 'Low' rather than 'None'.

sources.name: Johns Hopkins Medicine Health Library
sources.what: Condition and treatment articles plus renowned plain-English explainers on nutrition and 'healthy living' topics.
sources.notes: The 'Healthy Living' library (including their well-known sodium, sugar, and food-assignment explainers) is a standout.

sources.name: University of Michigan Health Library
sources.what: A large encyclopedia-style library of conditions, tests, medications, and self-care topics.
sources.notes: Quiet layout, essentially ad-free while reading; created with the Healthwise teaching library.

sources.name: Mount Sinai Health Library
sources.what: Categorized library of diseases, conditions, injuries, screenings, and drug information.
sources.notes: Includes alternative-medicine and herbal-supplement monographs that most hospital libraries skip.

sources.name: Mayo Clinic
sources.publisher: Mayo Foundation for Medical Education and Research
sources.what: Very thorough disease-and-symptom articles; the 'Diseases & Conditions' A-Z is encyclopedic.
sources.notes: Content quality is excellent and editorially independent, but the reading level runs a notch above MedlinePlus and you'll see banner ads and sponsor boxes around the content. Good second opinion, not a first stop for easy reading.

sources.name: MyPlate.gov (USDA)
sources.what: Free food-group guidance, printable MyPlate plans, recipes, and quizzes. No commercial ads at all.
sources.notes: Use the site fully without an account for guidance and printable plans. If you want the government tracker app, you create an account there — this directory points you to the reading site only.

sources.name: Medisafe (medication reminder)
sources.what: Freemium app for med schedules, refill reminders, and pill-interaction checks.
sources.notes: The free tier covers the core reminder job. Requires an account and collects usage/personal data (their privacy policy says so plainly). Review the privacy settings before syncing with family members.

sources.name: MyFitnessPal (meal tracker)
sources.what: The best-known free food and calorie tracker, with a huge community food database.
sources.notes: Free tier is genuinely usable for basic tracking. Expect account signup, ads in the free app, and substantial personal-data collection for its business model.

sources.name: Cronometer (meal/nutrition tracker)
sources.what: Free nutrition tracker that stands out for verified nutrient data instead of crowd-entered foods.
sources.notes: Free web version does the core job with fewer ads than rival free trackers. Account required; it stores diet data on their servers, so read the privacy policy.
